claim: A new mutant mouse (lamb1t) exhibits intermittent dystonic hindlimb movements and postures when awake.
source: A new mutant mouse (lamb1t) exhibits intermittent dystonic hindlimb movements and postures when awake, and hyperextension when asleep.
evidence: Described in abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with behavioral observations and videos

claim: The lamb1t mouse exhibits hyperextension when asleep.
source: A new mutant mouse (lamb1t) exhibits intermittent dystonic hindlimb movements and postures when awake, and hyperextension when asleep.
evidence: Described in abstract and demonstrated with sleep observations and videos

claim: Experiments showed co-contraction of opposing muscle groups in lamb1t mice.
source: Experiments showed co-contraction of opposing muscle groups, and indicated that symptoms depended on the interaction of brain and spinal cord.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMG recordings showing simultaneous activity in opposing muscles

claim: Symptoms in lamb1t mice depend on the interaction of brain and spinal cord.
source: Experiments showed co-contraction of opposing muscle groups, and indicated that symptoms depended on the interaction of brain and spinal cord.
evidence: Demonstrated by spinal transection experiments showing persistent activity after transection

claim: The dominant causative mutation in lamb1t was identified in the Lamb1 gene.
source: SNP mapping and exome sequencing identified the dominant causative mutation in the Lamb1 gene.
evidence: Identified through SNP mapping and exome sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing and co-segregation analysis

claim: Laminins are extracellular matrix proteins that are widely expressed.
source: Laminins are extracellular matrix proteins, widely expressed but also known to be important in synapse structure and plasticity.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about laminins

claim: Laminins are important in synapse structure and plasticity.
source: Laminins are extracellular matrix proteins, widely expressed but also known to be important in synapse structure and plasticity.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citations in the manuscript

claim: Awake recording in the cerebellum detected abnormal output from Purkinje cells during abnormal postures.
source: In accordance, awake recording in the cerebellum detected abnormal output from a circuit of two Lamb1-expressing neurons, Purkinje cells and their deep cerebellar nucleus targets, during abnormal postures.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo electrophysiology recordings in awake mice

claim: Awake recording in the cerebellum detected abnormal output from deep cerebellar nucleus neurons during abnormal postures.
source: In accordance, awake recording in the cerebellum detected abnormal output from a circuit of two Lamb1-expressing neurons, Purkinje cells and their deep cerebellar nucleus targets, during abnormal postures.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo electrophysiology recordings in awake mice

claim: Dystonia-like symptoms in lamb1t result from lapses in descending inhibition, exposing excess activity in intrinsic spinal circuits that coordinate muscles.
source: We propose that dystonia-like symptoms result from lapses in descending inhibition, exposing excess activity in intrinsic spinal circuits that coordinate muscles.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on spinal transection experiments and EMG data

claim: Dystonia is the third-most common human movement disorder.
source: Dystonia, the third-most common human movement disorder, involves 'sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal, often repetitive movements, postures or both' (Albanese et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Albanese et al., 2013

claim: Dystonia involves sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal, often repetitive movements, postures or both.
source: Dystonia, the third-most common human movement disorder, involves 'sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal, often repetitive movements, postures or both' (Albanese et al., 2013).
evidence: Clinical definition cited from Albanese et al., 2013

claim: There is strong evidence that dystonia is a circuit disorder involving various brain regions.
source: There is strong evidence that dystonia is a circuit disorder involving various brain regions, including sensory input, premotor and motor cortex, striatum and globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and parts of the thalamus, cerebellum, and the tracts connecting them (Berardelli et al., 1998; Breakefield et al., 2008; Lehéricy et al., 2013; Neychev et al., 2011; Quartarone and Hallett, 2013; Thompson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Dystonia involves decreased inhibition in synaptic plasticity.
source: There is also decreased inhibition and a bias toward potentiation in synaptic plasticity (Hallett, 2011; Quartarone and Pisani, 2011).
evidence: Cited from Hallett, 2011 and Quartarone and Pisani, 2011

claim: Dystonia involves a bias toward potentiation in synaptic plasticity.
source: There is also decreased inhibition and a bias toward potentiation in synaptic plasticity (Hallett, 2011; Quartarone and Pisani, 2011).
evidence: Cited from Hallett, 2011 and Quartarone and Pisani, 2011

claim: There has been a lack of a phenotypically penetrant genetically defined mouse model for dystonia.
source: Until recently, there has been a lack of a phenotypically penetrant genetically defined mouse model, where circuit hypotheses for mechanisms of dystonia can be tested in the context of abnormal movement (Liang et al., 2014; Weisheit and Dauer, 2015).
evidence: Cited from Liang et al., 2014 and Weisheit and Dauer, 2015

claim: The lamb1t mouse exhibits late postnatal/young adult onset of dystonia-like hindlimb movements and postures.
source: The lamb1t mouse introduced here exhibits late postnatal/young adult onset of dystonia-like hindlimb movements and postures, and it has high viability, gene penetrance, and inter-individual consistency.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral observations across multiple mice

claim: The lamb1t mouse has high viability, gene penetrance, and inter-individual consistency.
source: The lamb1t mouse introduced here exhibits late postnatal/young adult onset of dystonia-like hindlimb movements and postures, and it has high viability, gene penetrance, and inter-individual consistency.
evidence: Demonstrated by breeding data showing 51.5% of offspring with one WT parent were symptomatic

claim: The lamb1t mouse arose spontaneously in a WT C57Bl/6N mouse.
source: The lamb1t mouse arose spontaneously in a WT C57Bl/6N mouse.
evidence: Described in the origin and breeding section

claim: The lamb1t mutation shows dominant inheritance.
source: It showed dominant inheritance: 140 out of 272 (51.5%) mice with one WT parent were symptomatic.
evidence: Demonstrated by breeding data showing approximately 50% of offspring affected

claim: 140 out of 272 (51.5%) mice with one WT parent were symptomatic for lamb1t.
source: It showed dominant inheritance: 140 out of 272 (51.5%) mice with one WT parent were symptomatic.
evidence: Breeding data

claim: Awakening or novel environment typically elicited dystonic movements in lamb1t mice.
source: Awakening or novel environment typically elicited dystonic movements.
evidence: Behavioral observations documented in videos and text

claim: The most prominent symptom in lamb1t mice was hyperextension of one or both hindlimbs that was clearly hyperkinetic.
source: The most prominent was hyperextension of one or both hindlimbs that was clearly hyperkinetic.
evidence: Documented in behavioral observations and videos

claim: Motor behavior abnormalities in lamb1t mice included wide-spread (extended) legs during sitting.
source: Movement and postural abnormalities also included wide-spread (extended) legs during sitting, transiently curvy tail, strong hyperextension response to swimming, and abnormal tail suspension reflexes (Figure 1).
evidence: Documented in behavioral observations and Figure 1

claim: Motor behavior abnormalities in lamb1t mice included transiently curvy tail.
source: Movement and postural abnormalities also included wide-spread (extended) legs during sitting, transiently curvy tail, strong hyperextension response to swimming, and abnormal tail suspension reflexes (Figure 1).
evidence: Documented in behavioral observations and Figure 1

claim: Motor behavior abnormalities in lamb1t mice included strong hyperextension response to swimming.
source: Movement and postural abnormalities also included wide-spread (extended) legs during sitting, transiently curvy tail, strong hyperextension response to swimming, and abnormal tail suspension reflexes (Figure 1).
evidence: Documented in behavioral observations and Figure 1

claim: Motor behavior abnormalities in lamb1t mice included abnormal tail suspension reflexes.
source: Movement and postural abnormalities also included wide-spread (extended) legs during sitting, transiently curvy tail, strong hyperextension response to swimming, and abnormal tail suspension reflexes (Figure 1).
evidence: Documented in behavioral observations and Figure 1

claim: When unstressed in the home cage, lamb1t mice could walk normally.
source: When unstressed in the home cage, however, the mutant mice could walk normally, climb available structures, rear up while touching the side of the cage, and climb upside down on the food rack.
evidence: Behavioral observations

claim: Intermittency was a key feature of the impairment in lamb1t mice.
source: Dystonia in humans often has intermittent symptoms, and intermittency was a key feature of the impairment in the mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral observations showing variable symptom expression

claim: Motor symptoms in lamb1t mice were first detected between P17 and P28.
source: Motor symptoms were first detected between P17 and P28.
evidence: Developmental observations

claim: Between 2 and 6 months, symptoms in lamb1t mice became more persistent.
source: Between 2 and 6 months, symptoms became more persistent, and mice often slept with hindlimbs extended.
evidence: Longitudinal behavioral observations

claim: Brain, spinal cord, and spinal root morphology were indistinguishable from wild type in lamb1t mice.
source: Brain, spinal cord, and spinal root morphology were indistinguishable from wild type (WT), and weight gain was normal until motor symptoms become persistent.
evidence: Anatomical examination

claim: Weight gain was normal in lamb1t mice until motor symptoms become persistent.
source: Brain, spinal cord, and spinal root morphology were indistinguishable from wild type (WT), and weight gain was normal until motor symptoms become persistent.
evidence: Weight measurements over time

claim: During gentle manual assessment, hyperextended hindlimbs in lamb1t mice resisted motion at the joint.
source: During gentle manual assessment, hyperextended hindlimbs resisted motion at the joint.
evidence: Physical examination

claim: No cogwheel rigidity was felt in lamb1t mice.
source: No cogwheel rigidity (as in Parkinson's Disease) or rate-dependent resistance (as in spasticity) was felt.
evidence: Physical examination

claim: No rate-dependent resistance was felt in lamb1t mice.
source: No cogwheel rigidity (as in Parkinson's Disease) or rate-dependent resistance (as in spasticity) was felt.
evidence: Physical examination

claim: Hindlimb stretch reflexes in lamb1t mice were present when the hindlimb was relaxed but suppressed when it was hyperextended.
source: Hindlimb stretch reflexes, elicited by slowly pulling on a foot, were present when the hindlimb was relaxed but suppressed when it was hyperextended.
evidence: Physical examination

claim: No abnormality was detected in the back, forelimbs, head, or axial posture of lamb1t mice.
source: We detected no abnormality in the back, forelimbs, head, or axial posture, and the mice groomed and built nests well.
evidence: Behavioral observations

claim: Lamb1t mice groomed and built nests well.
source: We detected no abnormality in the back, forelimbs, head, or axial posture, and the mice groomed and built nests well.
evidence: Behavioral observations

claim: Social interactions appeared unexceptional in lamb1t mice.
source: Social interactions appeared unexceptional, and both sexes bred successfully.
evidence: Behavioral observations

claim: Both sexes of lamb1t mice bred successfully.
source: Social interactions appeared unexceptional, and both sexes bred successfully.
evidence: Breeding data

claim: The time to cross the beam was similar when WT and lamb1t mice were compared.
source: The time to cross the beam was similar when WT and mutant mice were compared, but mutants exhibited many more hindlimb slips (Figure 3A), sometimes pulled with their forelimbs (Video 1), and when very affected sometimes could not stay on the beam.
evidence: Elevated beam test data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Lamb1t mice exhibited many more hindlimb slips than WT on the elevated beam.
source: The time to cross the beam was similar when WT and mutant mice were compared, but mutants exhibited many more hindlimb slips (Figure 3A), sometimes pulled with their forelimbs (Video 1), and when very affected sometimes could not stay on the beam.
evidence: Elevated beam test data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Lamb1t mice stayed on the rotarod 40% as long as WT.
source: Lamb1t mice stayed on the rod 40% as long as WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: Rotarod test data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Lamb1t mice were significantly slower than WT in the Olympic pool test.
source: Mutants were significantly slower (mutant [6.9 ± 0.49 s] and WT [2.46 ± 0.07 s], p = 4.5 x 10−12 by t-test; n = 27 WT and 28 mutant mice), but swim speed did not decline with age or weight (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Olympic pool test data with statistical analysis

claim: Swim speed in lamb1t mice did not decline with age or weight.
source: Mutants were significantly slower (mutant [6.9 ± 0.49 s] and WT [2.46 ± 0.07 s], p = 4.5 x 10−12 by t-test; n = 27 WT and 28 mutant mice), but swim speed did not decline with age or weight (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Olympic pool test data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: There was no difference in horizontal or ambulatory activity between WT and lamb1t mice for either sex in the activity chamber.
source: There was no difference in either horizontal (same beam) or ambulatory activity (different beams broken successively) between WT and mutants for either sex; that is, motor impairment did not diminish activity (two-way ANOVA, p = 0.81 males, p = 0.40 females. n = 22 WT [9 males and 13 females]; n = 20 lamb1t [10 males and 10 females]).
evidence: Activity chamber test data with statistical analysis

claim: No difference in forelimb function was detected in the adhesive removal test between WT and lamb1t mice.
source: No difference in forelimb function was detected in the adhesive removal test (sticker applied to the forehead) (Student's two-tailed t-test, p = 0.40, n = 16 per group, average age 77 days).
evidence: Adhesive removal test data with statistical analysis

claim: Sciatic nerve conduction velocity in lamb1t mice was in the normal range (40 to 50 m/s).
source: Sciatic nerve conduction velocity (mediated by fast myelinated axons) in anesthetized mice was measured with EMG electrodes, and it was in the normal range (40 to 50 m/s, n = 3, both legs, for WT and mutant).
evidence: Nerve conduction velocity measurements

claim: Cross sections of fixed sciatic nerve showed a normal distribution of myelinated axons in lamb1t mice.
source: Cross sections of fixed sciatic nerve (mid-thigh) showed a normal distribution of myelinated axons by toluidine blue or hematoxylin-eosin stain.
evidence: Histological examination

claim: WT and lamb1t mice had normal-appearing large and small myelinated fibers and unmyelinated fibers in sciatic nerve.
source: Both WT and mutant had normal-appearing large and small myelinated fibers and unmyelinated fibers.
evidence: Histological examination

claim: Time to tail flick was not significantly different between WT and lamb1t mice in the tail immersion test.
source: Time to tail flick was measured in water at 51oC. Male mice had longer average latencies to tail withdrawal than females; however, WT and mutant were not significantly different (male WT 1.99 s ± 0.21; male mutant 2.07 s ± 0.23; female WT 1.44 ± 0.19; female mutant 1.50 ± 0.14; mean ± SEM; male n =15 for WT and 13 for mutant; female n =9 for WT and 14 for mutant, two-way ANOVA, p =0.0092 for sex difference, and p = 0.75 for genotype effect).
evidence: Tail immersion test data with statistical analysis

claim: Male mice had longer average latencies to tail withdrawal than females in the tail immersion test.
source: Time to tail flick was measured in water at 51oC. Male mice had longer average latencies to tail withdrawal than females; however, WT and mutant were not significantly different (male WT 1.99 s ± 0.21; male mutant 2.07 s ± 0.23; female WT 1.44 ± 0.19; female mutant 1.50 ± 0.14; mean ± SEM; male n =15 for WT and 13 for mutant; female n =9 for WT and 14 for mutant, two-way ANOVA, p =0.0092 for sex difference, and p = 0.75 for genotype effect).
evidence: Tail immersion test data with statistical analysis

claim: Twitching of hindlimbs during sleep was seen in lamb1t mice.
source: In sleep and in isoflurane anesthesia, twitching of lamb1t hindlimbs was often seen when mice were old enough for symptoms to be firmly established (Video 3).
evidence: Sleep observations documented in Video 3

claim: Twitching of hindlimbs was seen in lamb1t mice under isoflurane anesthesia.
source: In sleep and in isoflurane anesthesia, twitching of lamb1t hindlimbs was often seen when mice were old enough for symptoms to be firmly established (Video 3).
evidence: Anesthesia observations documented in Video 3

claim: Twitching during sleep in lamb1t mice was seen in 76 of 150 hourly observations where the mouse appeared to be asleep.
source: Twitching of hindlimbs during sleep was assessed at hourly intervals through the bottoms of cages with scant litter in 31 mutant mice, average 14.5 weeks old. Twitching was seen in 76 of 150 hourly observations where the mouse appeared to be asleep, indicating that it too is intermittent.
evidence: Sleep observation data

claim: EMG recordings ruled out myotonia in lamb1t mice.
source: Electrode recordings ruled out myotonia (persistent muscle firing causing prolonged contractions because of defective Cl- channels), because characteristic muscle fiber potentials (positive sharp waves and/or fibrillation potentials) with waxing and waning frequency and amplitude (Heller et al., 1982) were not detected, and there were periods of normal electrical silence (Figure 4A).
evidence: EMG data shown in Figure 4A with citation to Heller et al., 1982

claim: EMG recordings ruled out neuromyotonia in lamb1t mice.
source: The recordings also ruled out neuromyotonia (peripheral nerve hyperexcitability) and myokymia (quivering of muscles) because of the absence of either of their EMG signatures, a constant buzz of neuromuscular junction activity (Isaacs, 1961; Stum et al., 2008), or regular motor unit action potential activity in multiplet discharges (Toyka et al., 1997; Zielasek et al., 2000).
evidence: EMG data with citations to Isaacs, 1961; Stum et al., 2008; Toyka et al., 1997; Zielasek et al., 2000

claim: EMG recordings ruled out myokymia in lamb1t mice.
source: The recordings also ruled out neuromyotonia (peripheral nerve hyperexcitability) and myokymia (quivering of muscles) because of the absence of either of their EMG signatures, a constant buzz of neuromuscular junction activity (Isaacs, 1961; Stum et al., 2008), or regular motor unit action potential activity in multiplet discharges (Toyka et al., 1997; Zielasek et al., 2000).
evidence: EMG data with citations

claim: No signs of myopathy were detected in lamb1t mice.
source: We also did not detect signs of myopathy (muscle weakness), such as low-amplitude, short duration motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) (Hanisch et al., 2014).
evidence: EMG data with citation to Hanisch et al., 2014

claim: Plasma creatine kinase was normal in lamb1t mice.
source: Plasma creatine kinase was also normal (n = 3 WT and 4 lamb1t), that is, there was no indication of muscular dystrophy.
evidence: Plasma creatine kinase measurements

claim: Two-electrode EMG recorded co-contraction driven by motor unit activity in lamb1t mice.
source: Notably, two-electrode EMG recorded co-contraction driven by motor unit activity. Synchronized MUAPs, typically at 10 Hz, were detected with recordings from opposing (agonist and antagonist) muscles (Figure 4B,D,F).
evidence: EMG data shown in Figure 4B,D,F

claim: Synchronized MUAPs, typically at 10 Hz, were detected with recordings from opposing muscles in lamb1t mice.
source: Notably, two-electrode EMG recorded co-contraction driven by motor unit activity. Synchronized MUAPs, typically at 10 Hz, were detected with recordings from opposing (agonist and antagonist) muscles (Figure 4B,D,F).
evidence: EMG data shown in Figure 4B,D,F

claim: Synchronized polyphasic bursts in lamb1t mice were very similar to those seen in sleeping blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia patients.
source: Synchronized polyphasic bursts very similar to those seen in sleeping blepharospasm (eyelid) and oromandibular (mouth, jaw, and tongue) dystonia patients (Sforza et al., 1991) correlated with twitching movements (Figure 4C,D,E).
evidence: EMG data shown in Figure 4C,D,E with citation to Sforza et al., 1991

claim: No correlation of firing was observed when electrodes were moved to the same muscles on contralateral legs in lamb1t mice.
source: To test whether co-contraction was due to a system-wide volley of excessive descending activation, electrodes were moved to the same muscles on contralateral legs or to opposing muscles on contralateral legs. No correlation of firing was observed in either case (example in Figure 4G).
evidence: EMG data shown in Figure 4G

claim: No correlation of firing was observed when electrodes were moved to opposing muscles on contralateral legs in lamb1t mice.
source: To test whether co-contraction was due to a system-wide volley of excessive descending activation, electrodes were moved to the same muscles on contralateral legs or to opposing muscles on contralateral legs. No correlation of firing was observed in either case (example in Figure 4G).
evidence: EMG data shown in Figure 4G

claim: In all lamb1t mice tested, the EMG activity observed under anesthesia was undiminished or slightly enhanced by spinal transection.
source: We performed this on six lamb1t mice and four WT. In all mutant mice, the activity observed under anesthesia was undiminished or slightly enhanced by spinal transection (Video 5).
evidence: Spinal transection experiment data shown in Video 5

claim: WT mice remained immobile under anesthesia before and after spinal transection.
source: WT mice remained immobile under anesthesia before and after transection.
evidence: Spinal transection experiment data

claim: The spinal transection observations rule out the possibility that the co-contraction originates in the brain.
source: These observations are instructive for the mechanism of the disorder, because they rule out the possibility that the co-contraction originates in the brain.
evidence: Inference from spinal transection experiment results

claim: The spinal transection observations demonstrate aberrant intrinsic spinal activity in lamb1t mice.
source: They also demonstrate aberrant intrinsic spinal activity and suggest that co-contraction is determined by the over-activation of propriospinal circuits designed to execute or oppose reflexes, motion or postural stability.
evidence: Inference from spinal transection experiment results

claim: Co-contraction in lamb1t mice is determined by the over-activation of propriospinal circuits designed to execute or oppose reflexes, motion or postural stability.
source: They also demonstrate aberrant intrinsic spinal activity and suggest that co-contraction is determined by the over-activation of propriospinal circuits designed to execute or oppose reflexes, motion or postural stability.
evidence: Inference from spinal transection experiment results

claim: For 24 individual SNP-mapped symptomatic hybrid mice only one B6 region was shared by all.
source: For 24 individual SNP-mapped symptomatic hybrid mice only one B6 region was shared by all.
evidence: SNP mapping data

claim: The defining recombination events restricted the locus to the first 35 gigabases of chromosome 12.
source: The defining recombination events restricted the locus to the first 35 gigabases of chromosome 12 (Figure 5A).
evidence: SNP mapping data shown in Figure 5A

claim: There were nine mutant-specific variants in the chromosome 12 locus identified by exome sequencing.
source: There were nine mutant-specific variants in the chromosome 12 locus, but only one was a non-synonymous coding change.
evidence: Exome sequencing data

claim: Only one variant in the chromosome 12 locus was a non-synonymous coding change.
source: There were nine mutant-specific variants in the chromosome 12 locus, but only one was a non-synonymous coding change.
evidence: Exome sequencing data

claim: The candidate mutation was a single base pair transversion in Lamb1 (T5460A) that changed a leucine to a stop codon, amino acid p.Leu1730stop.
source: The candidate was near the closest recombination site (Figure 5A) and was a single base pair transversion in Lamb1 (T5460A) that changed a leucine to a stop codon, amino acid p.Leu1730stop (Figure 5B).
evidence: Exome sequencing data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
source: The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 5C) and validated by showing complete co-segregation between the mutation and the symptoms in eight littermates on the C57Bl/6 background (four with symptoms, four without), and six littermates on the mixed C57Bl/6-FVB background (three with symptoms, three without), p < 10−8 by two-tailed t-test.
evidence: Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The mutation was validated by showing complete co-segregation between the mutation and the symptoms.
source: The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 5C) and validated by showing complete co-segregation between the mutation and the symptoms in eight littermates on the C57Bl/6 background (four with symptoms, four without), and six littermates on the mixed C57Bl/6-FVB background (three with symptoms, three without), p < 10−8 by two-tailed t-test.
evidence: Co-segregation analysis with statistical significance

claim: Average litter size compared to WT x het litters was reduced 28% in het x het crosses of FVB-B6 hybrids.
source: 25% of offspring of het x het crosses of FVB-B6 hybrids should have had two copies of the mutation, but instead average litter size compared to WT x het litters was reduced 28% (mean ± SEM; n = 255 mutant x WT offspring; n = 178 mutant x mutant offspring. p = 7.9 x 10−5, Student's two-tailed t-test).
evidence: Breeding data with statistical analysis

claim: No homozygotes were found by genotyping 16 dead pups or 4 surviving runts.
source: No homozygotes were found by genotyping 16 dead pups or 4 surviving runts.
evidence: Genotyping data

claim: SNP mapping on 16 hybrids with robust symptoms showed all were heterozygous for the chromosome 12 locus.
source: Intercrossing did produce some hybrids with symptoms as robust as B6 lamb1t, however, and we performed SNP mapping on 16 of those to look for homozygotes: all were heterozygous for the chromosome 12 locus.
evidence: SNP mapping data

claim: Homozygosity for the lamb1t mutation is lethal.
source: This is further evidence that homozygosity is lethal and supports the influence of unlinked modifier genes that increase or decrease symptom strength.
evidence: Inference from breeding and genotyping data

claim: Laminin is a trimer of three different subunits that form a cross when assembled.
source: Laminin is a trimer of three different subunits that form a cross when assembled (Figure 6A) (Hohenester and Yurchenco, 2013).
evidence: Cited from Hohenester and Yurchenco, 2013 and shown in Figure 6A

claim: The lamb1t premature stop codon deletes the last 57 amino acids from β1's coiled-coil domain.
source: The lamb1t premature stop codon deletes the last 57 amino acids from β1's coiled-coil domain.
evidence: Inference from mutation position and protein structure

claim: The lamb1t mutation is in exon 32, just 36 bases upstream of the next (and final) exon junction.
source: The lamb1t mutation is in exon 32, just 36 bases upstream of the next (and final) exon junction.
evidence: Gene structure analysis

claim: When a stop codon is less than 50 bases from the final exon junction, the mRNA escapes nonsense-mediated decay.
source: Cells have a mechanism for degrading mRNA with premature stop codons, but when a stop codon is less than 50 bases from the final exon junction, the mRNA escapes nonsense-mediated decay (Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012).
evidence: Cited from Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012

claim: The truncated laminin β1 form in lamb1t should be ~6 kDa smaller than wild type.
source: The truncated form should be ~6 kDa smaller, and it was resolved when electrophoresis time was extended (Figure 6B).
evidence: Calculation based on amino acid deletion and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The truncated laminin β1 form was resolved when electrophoresis time was extended.
source: The truncated form should be ~6 kDa smaller, and it was resolved when electrophoresis time was extended (Figure 6B).
evidence: Immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B

claim: No reduction in laminin β1 levels was observed in lamb1t mice.
source: In agreement with the proposal that the truncated protein is fully expressed, we did not observe a reduction in laminin β1 levels (Figure 6B); we also saw no reduction in samples from cerebellum and sciatic nerve (not shown).
evidence: Immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B

claim: MultiCoil predicted no change in coiled coil propensity for the majority of coil upstream of the truncation in lamb1t.
source: Whether the truncation should disrupt the coiled coil was predicted with MultiCoil. No change was calculated for the majority of coil upstream of the truncation (Figure 6C), implying that mutant β1 should assemble with laminin alpha and gamma subunits.
evidence: MultiCoil computational analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Mutant laminin β1 should assemble with laminin alpha and gamma subunits.
source: Whether the truncation should disrupt the coiled coil was predicted with MultiCoil. No change was calculated for the majority of coil upstream of the truncation (Figure 6C), implying that mutant β1 should assemble with laminin alpha and gamma subunits.
evidence: Inference from MultiCoil analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Lamb1 is expressed in several sites implicated in movement disorders.
source: Lamb1 is expressed in several sites implicated in movement disorders, including sites that showed neuropathology in rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (RDP) (Oblak et al., 2014).
evidence: Expression data from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT with citation to Oblak et al., 2014

claim: Lamb1 is expressed in substantia nigra compacta.
source: These include substantia nigra compacta, cerebellar Purkinje neurons, and the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN).
evidence: Expression data from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: Lamb1 is expressed in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: These include substantia nigra compacta, cerebellar Purkinje neurons, and the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN).
evidence: Expression data from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: Lamb1 is expressed in the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN).
source: These include substantia nigra compacta, cerebellar Purkinje neurons, and the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN).
evidence: Expression data from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: Lamb1 is expressed in the striatum in a discrete population of interneurons.
source: Lamb1 is also expressed in the striatum, where the low density of labeled cells indicates a discrete population of interneurons (Figure 7A).
evidence: Expression data shown in Figure 7A from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: Lamb1 is expressed in inhibitory inputs from molecular layer cells that probably are basket and stellate cells.
source: Lamb1 seems to not be expressed in some excitatory inputs to Purkinje cells (granule cells, or the inferior olivary nucleus, Figure 7D) but is expressed in inhibitory inputs from molecular layer cells that probably are basket and stellate cells (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Expression data shown in Figure 7B,C,D from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: Lamb1 is not expressed in granule cells.
source: Lamb1 seems to not be expressed in some excitatory inputs to Purkinje cells (granule cells, or the inferior olivary nucleus, Figure 7D) but is expressed in inhibitory inputs from molecular layer cells that probably are basket and stellate cells (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Expression data shown in Figure 7B,C,D from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: Lamb1 is not expressed in the inferior olivary nucleus.
source: Lamb1 seems to not be expressed in some excitatory inputs to Purkinje cells (granule cells, or the inferior olivary nucleus, Figure 7D) but is expressed in inhibitory inputs from molecular layer cells that probably are basket and stellate cells (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Expression data shown in Figure 7D from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: In the spinal cord, there is diffuse Lamb1 stain in lamina 1.
source: In the spinal cord, there is diffuse stain in lamina 1, and strong expression in a sparse population of interneurons in lamina 2 or 3 of the dorsal horn (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: Expression data shown in Figure 7E-G from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: There is strong Lamb1 expression in a sparse population of interneurons in lamina 2 or 3 of the dorsal horn.
source: In the spinal cord, there is diffuse stain in lamina 1, and strong expression in a sparse population of interneurons in lamina 2 or 3 of the dorsal horn (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: Expression data shown in Figure 7E-G from Allen Brain Atlas and GENSAT

claim: Motor neurons appear to have little or no mRNA for Lamb1.

claim: Single-unit extracellular recordings revealed irregularly firing neurons during abnormal postures in lamb1t mice compared to WT.
source: Single-unit extracellular recordings of spontaneous activity of Purkinje cells and cells in the DCN were performed in awake head-restrained mice. Figure 8 presents the data as box and whisker plots to show differences in median, interquartile range, and skew, while Table 1 has the calculated means and statistical differences. Recordings revealed irregularly firing neurons during abnormal postures in the lamb1t mice compared to WT (Figure 8A,E).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8A,E

claim: The average firing rate was decreased in the DCN in lamb1t mice during abnormal postures.
source: The average firing rate (defined as the number of spikes divided by the recorded time) was decreased in the DCN in the mutant during abnormal postures, whereas there was no significant difference between the WT and the mutant during normal postures (Figure 8B).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8B

claim: There was no significant difference in average firing rate between WT and lamb1t DCN neurons during normal postures.
source: The average firing rate (defined as the number of spikes divided by the recorded time) was decreased in the DCN in the mutant during abnormal postures, whereas there was no significant difference between the WT and the mutant during normal postures (Figure 8B).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8B

claim: The predominant firing rate of DCN cells in lamb1t mice was significantly higher during both normal and abnormal postures compared to WT.
source: The predominant firing rate (defined as the reciprocal of the mode interspike interval) of the mutant mice was significantly higher during both normal and abnormal postures compared to WT, but highest with abnormal postures (Figure 8C).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8C

claim: There was a significant increase in the CV ISI of DCN cells in lamb1t mice during abnormal postures compared to WT or to mutants during normal postures.
source: To measure the irregularity of firing in all conditions, the coefficient of variation of the interspike interval (CV ISI), defined as the standard deviation of the interspike interval divided by its mean, was calculated. There was a significant increase in the CV ISI of DCN cells in the mutant during abnormal postures compared to WT or to mutants during normal postures, confirming that cells in the DCN of mutant animals fire irregularly during abnormal postures.
evidence: Electrophysiology data with statistical analysis

claim: Purkinje cells in lamb1t mice fire irregularly during abnormal postures when compared to WT mice.
source: Similar to cells in the DCN, Purkinje cells in mutant mice appeared to fire irregularly during abnormal postures when compared to WT mice (Figure 8E).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8E

claim: The average firing rate of Purkinje cells was statistically higher in lamb1t mice during normal postures compared to WT.
source: Like in the DCN, average rate was higher in lamb1t during normal postures, but was similar to WT, not lower, when abnormal postures were present (Figure 8F).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8F

claim: The predominant firing rate of Purkinje cells in lamb1t mice was higher during both normal and abnormal postures than in WT.
source: The predominant firing rate in mutants was higher during both normal and abnormal postures than in WT (Figure 8G).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8G

claim: The CV ISI of Purkinje cells in lamb1t mice during normal postures was not significantly different from WT.

evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8H

claim: The CV ISI of Purkinje cells in lamb1t mice during abnormal postures was much higher than WT.
source: Also like in the DCN, the CV ISI of mutants during normal postures was not significantly different from WT, but during abnormal postures CV ISI was much higher (Figure 8H).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8H

claim: Purkinje cells and cells in the DCN of the lamb1t mouse fire irregularly with high-frequency bursts during abnormal postures.
